subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
extraLines: 1. What is Physics?
Physics is the branch of science concerned with the nature and properties of matter and
energy. Its subject matter includes mechanics, heat, light and other radiation, sound,
electricity, magnetism, and the structure of atoms.
2. Define classical mechanics.
Classical mechanics is the branch of physics that describes the motion of macroscopic
(everyday) objects and how their motion changes because of the forces acting on them.
3. A bike accelerates uniformly from rest to a speed of 7.10 m/s over a distance of
35.4 m. Determine the acceleration of the bike.

4. If you know the position vectors of a particle at two points along its path and
also know the time it took to move from one point to the other, can you determine
the particle's instantaneous velocity? Its average velocity? Explain.
The average velocity can be determined: it is the displacement divided by the time interval,
v_avg = (r2 − r1) / Δt. The instantaneous velocity cannot be determined from just these two
positions, because it is the limit of the average velocity as the time interval shrinks to zero (v
= dr/dt); that requires knowing the positions at two very close instants, or the position as a
function of time.
5. If a train of freight cars, each 10 m long, rolls by you at the rate of three cars
each second, what is the speed of the train?
In one second, three cars — a length of 3 × 10 m = 30 m — pass by. So the speed of the
train is 30 m/s.
6. Why does a book sitting on a table never accelerate "spontaneously" in
response to the trillions of inter-atomic forces acting within it?
The inter-atomic forces inside the book are internal forces. By Newton's third law they occur
in equal and opposite pairs, so they cancel out and cannot accelerate the book as a whole.
The only external forces on the book — its weight and the upward normal force from the
table — are also balanced, so the net force is zero and the book stays at rest.
7. A table-tennis ball is thrown at a stationary bowling ball. The table-tennis ball
makes a one-dimensional elastic collision and bounces back along the same line.
After the collision, compared to the bowling ball, the table-tennis ball has: (a) a
larger magnitude of momentum and more kinetic energy (b) a smaller magnitude
of momentum and more kinetic energy (c) a larger magnitude of momentum and
less kinetic energy (d) a smaller magnitude of momentum and less kinetic energy.
Answer (b). Because the table-tennis ball is very light compared with the bowling ball, it
rebounds with nearly its original speed, while the bowling ball creeps forward slowly. The
bowling ball nevertheless carries the larger momentum (about twice the ball's, since
momentum is conserved and the ball's momentum reverses), whereas almost all of the
kinetic energy stays with the light ball — so the table-tennis ball has a smaller magnitude of
momentum and more kinetic energy than the bowling ball.
8. Rank an automobile dashboard, seatbelt, and airbag in terms of (a) the impulse
and (b) the average force they deliver to a front-seat passenger during a collision,
from greatest to least.
(a) Impulse: all three are equal. Each must bring the passenger to rest, so each delivers the
same change of momentum, and impulse equals change of momentum. (b) Average force:
dashboard greatest, then seatbelt, then airbag least. Since impulse = average force ×
collision time, the device that stops the passenger in the shortest time (the hard dashboard)
exerts the greatest average force, while the airbag stretches the stopping time the most and
so exerts the smallest average force.
9. Three balls are thrown into the air simultaneously. What is the acceleration of
their center of mass while they are in motion?
The only external force on the system is gravity (air resistance neglected), so the center of
mass accelerates exactly like a single particle in free fall: its acceleration is g ≈ 9.8 m/s²,
directed vertically downward, regardless of the individual motions of the three balls.
10. When a car drives off a cliff, why does it rotate forward as it falls?
As the car leaves the cliff, its front wheels go over the edge first and the front end begins to
fall while the rear wheels are still supported. This starts the car rotating forward about its
rear axle, so by the time it is fully airborne it already has a forward rotation, which continues
as it falls.
11. If you walk along the top of a fence, why does holding your arms out help you
to keep your balance?
Holding your arms out increases your rotational inertia (moment of inertia) about the axis
along the fence. A larger rotational inertia means any tipping rotation develops more slowly,
giving you time to shift your weight and correct your balance; the outstretched arms also let
you move your center of mass back over the fence.
12. What does it mean to say that angular momentum is conserved?
It means that the total angular momentum of a system remains constant — it does not
change with time — provided no net external torque acts on the system. Internal torques
may redistribute angular momentum among the parts of the system, but the total stays the
same.
13. (a) What angle in radians is subtended by an arc 1.50 m in length on the
circumference of a circle of radius 2.50 m? What is this angle in degrees? (b) An
arc 14.0 cm in length on the circumference of a circle subtends an angle of 128°.
What is the radius of the circle? (c) The angle between two radii of a circle with
radius 1.50 m is 0.700 rad. What length of arc is intercepted on the circumference
of the circle by the two radii?

15. A bus's tire rotates at an initial angular speed of 20.5 rad/s. The driver
accelerates, and after 4.5 s the tire's angular speed is 29.0 rad/s. What is the
tire's average angular acceleration during the 4.5 s time interval?
Average angular acceleration α = Δω / Δt = (29.0 − 20.5) / 4.5 = 8.5 / 4.5 ≈ 1.89 rad/s².
16. Two people are carrying a uniform wooden board that is 3.00 m long and
weighs 160 N. If one person applies an upward force equal to 60 N at one end, at
what point does the other person lift?
The board is in equilibrium, so both the net force and the net torque on it are zero. Force
balance: F1 + F2 − W = 0, so the second person lifts with F2 = 160 − 60 = 100 N. Torque
balance about the end where the 60 N force acts (the weight acts at the midpoint, 1.50 m
from either end): F2 × d = W × (L/2) = 160 × 1.50 = 240 N·m, giving d = 240 / 100 = 2.4 m.
The other person lifts at a point 2.4 m from the first person's end, i.e. 0.6 m from his own
end of the board.

18. Does Archimedes' principle tell us that, if an immersed object displaces liquid
weighing 10 N, the buoyant force on the object is 10 N?
Yes. Archimedes' principle states that the buoyant force on an immersed (or floating) object
is equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. If the object displaces liquid weighing 10 N,
the buoyant force on it is exactly 10 N, directed upward.
19. Define tangential stress. Is there any difference between tangential and
shearing stress?
Tangential stress is the deforming force per unit area acting parallel (tangent) to the surface
of a body, tending to make one layer of the body slide over another. There is no difference:
tangential stress and shearing stress are two names for the same quantity.
20. Define elasticity and plasticity, and give some examples of materials that
show each property.
Elasticity is the property of a material by virtue of which it regains its original shape and size
after the deforming force is removed (within the elastic limit); examples: steel, rubber, and a
stretched spring. Plasticity is the property by virtue of which a material undergoes a
permanent deformation and does not return to its original shape when the deforming force is
removed; examples: clay, plasticine, putty, and wet dough. Many materials, such as copper
and aluminium, behave elastically for small stresses and plastically beyond the yield point.
21. Explain the following terms: steady flow, unsteady flow, compressible fluid,
incompressible fluid and viscous fluid.
Steady flow: the velocity of the fluid at any fixed point does not change with time. Unsteady
flow: the velocity at a point changes with time. Compressible fluid: a fluid whose density
(volume) changes appreciably when pressure is applied, e.g. a gas. Incompressible fluid: a
fluid whose density stays essentially constant under pressure, e.g. water and most liquids.
Viscous fluid: a fluid that offers internal friction (viscosity) between its layers as they move
relative to each other, e.g. honey or engine oil.
22. Define stress. Is it a vector quantity?
Stress is the internal restoring force developed per unit area of a body when a deforming
force is applied to it (stress = force / area; SI unit N/m², the pascal). No — stress is not a
vector quantity. It is a tensor quantity, because describing it requires the magnitude and
direction of the force as well as the orientation of the surface on which it acts.
23. 'Captain Planet' is somewhere between galaxies. When a gong sounds in a
neighboring spaceship, Captain reacts to the sound. What is wrong with this
scenario?
Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium (such as air) to travel. The space
between galaxies is essentially a vacuum — there is no air or other medium there — so the
sound of the gong could never reach him. No medium, no sound.
24. (a) "A 20 dB sound is twice as intense as a 10 dB sound." Explain. (b) The
degree of Doppler shift experienced by a listener is independent of how far the
listener is from a moving sound source. Is it true or wrong? Explain.
(a) The statement is wrong. The decibel scale is logarithmic: β = 10 log (I / I₀), so every
increase of 10 dB means the intensity becomes 10 times greater. A 20 dB sound is therefore
10 times — not twice — as intense as a 10 dB sound. (b) True. The Doppler shift depends
only on the speeds of the source and the listener relative to the medium (the relative motion
along the line joining them), not on the distance between them; changing the distance
changes the loudness, not the observed frequency shift.
25. Charge is also said to be conserved. What does it mean? Explain.
Charge conservation means that the net electric charge is never created or destroyed; it can
only be transferred from one body to another. In any process, the total charge at an earlier
time is equal to the total charge at a later time — the change in the amount of charge in any
volume is exactly equal to the amount of charge that flows into or out of that volume.
